name: Kemalism
summary: Kemalism is the founding ideology of the Turkish Republic, the six principles of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk: republicanism, nationalism, populism, statism, secularism and revolution. In practice it meant a state-led economy with state enterprises and planning, rapid top-down reform that abolished the caliphate, religious courts and religious dress in public, equal civil and political rights for women, a unitary nation defined by citizenship, and rule by one party that closed its opposition. It rejected class struggle for a solidarist, classless ideal and renounced pan-Islamic and pan-Turkish expansion.
scope: The Kemalism of Atatürk's presidency (1923-1938) and the CHP of the one-party period, as Britannica, the Tarsus American College summaries of the principles and reforms, Abidor and Erdoğan describe them, with Atatürk's 1927 speech and tenth-anniversary address and the 1924 constitution as primary texts. Britannica names the six principles as Kemalism, enshrined in the CHP programme of 1931 and the constitution of 1937. It excludes the later Islamist, centre-left CHP and military-guardian variants.

sources.usedFor: The 1924 constitution as a vehicle of Kemalism, with the Grand National Assembly at the centre and the separation of powers eroded.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Article 69 of the 1924 constitution declares all privileges claimed by groups, classes, families and individuals abolished and forbidden.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The 1924 constitution says no one may be molested on account of religion, sect, ritual or philosophic convictions.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: Atatuerk's speech of 1927 says the nation would prefer to die rather than live in slavery, and answers with the slogan "Independence or death".

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1924 constitution says no public funds may be spent except as provided in the Budget or authorised by special law, and the Assembly examines and ratifies the budget.

civil-marriage.rationale: Britannica records the adoption of a purely secular system of family law, replacing religious courts.

civilizational-union.rationale: Britannica records that the republic renounced Pan-Islamic, Pan-Turkish and Pan-Ottoman goals in foreign policy.

class-collaboration.rationale: Erdogan reports that the CHP cadres chose a solidarist ideal of a classless society over a class-based view, and that its 1935 programme banned organisations founded on class and class struggle.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Erdogan reports that the CHP adopted a solidarist "classless society" ideal instead of a class-based view, and its 1935 programme banned organisations founded on class struggle.

clerical-rule.rationale: Britannica records the abolition of the caliphate, of religious courts and schools, and of the dervish orders, which struck down clerical authority.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Britannica records the renunciation of Pan-Turkish goals and the acceptance of the loss of Mosul in 1926.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The 1924 constitution declares that sovereignty belongs without restriction to the nation and that the Assembly exercises it in the nation's name.

death-penalty.rationale: Abidor records that the Independence Tribunals executed the recalcitrant.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The 1924 constitution has the Assembly, not the voters, elect the President of the Republic.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The 1924 constitution declares that sovereignty belongs without restriction to the nation.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Erdogan records that the revolutions of 1922-1928 liquidated the monarchic institutions inherited from the Ottomans.

elective-rulers.rationale: The 1924 constitution has the Grand National Assembly elect the President of the Republic, who is head of the state.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The 1924 constitution lets the Council of Commissioners decree martial law for a month, suspending or restricting the inviolability of the person, the home and the press, subject to the Assembly's approval.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Article 69 of the 1924 constitution says all Turks are equal before the law; it speaks of Turks, defined by citizenship regardless of race or religion.

gradual-change.rationale: Abidor records that Atatuerk meant to drag Turkey "immediately and completely" into the modern, and that the alphabet and calendar changes were imposed at once.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The 1924 constitution vests supreme command of the army in the Grand National Assembly, represented by the President, with command in peacetime entrusted to the Chief of Staff.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Under the 1924 constitution the Assembly may dissolve itself by absolute majority; no power to dissolve it is given to the President.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Britannica records changes in school curricula and the rewriting of history to glorify the Turkish past.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Britannica records that the republic renounced Pan-Islamic, Pan-Turkish and Pan-Ottoman goals in foreign policy.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Britannica records the abolition of religious courts and schools in 1924, which ended scripture as a source of law.

leader-cult.rationale: Britannica describes Atatuerk's "autocratic, dominating, and inspiring personality" as directing and shaping the republic and records the title of "Father of Turks"; Abidor records that the name Atatuerk, "Father Turk", was given to him alone.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The republic built state enterprises and planning in the 1930s (Britannica) and, in the account of Erdogan, nationalised many foreign concession companies; private enterprise stayed, so the answer is moderate.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The Atatuerk centre says Kemalist nationalism holds that the Turkish state is an indivisible whole comprising its territory and people.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Erdogan records that the revolutions of 1922-1928 liquidated the monarchic and theocratic institutions inherited from the Ottomans.

more-religion-public.rationale: Abidor says religion "has no role in the Turkish polity" and records the bans on the fez and the headscarf; Britannica adds the ban on clerical garb outside places of worship in 1934.

national-resource-control.rationale: Erdogan records that the statist policies of the 1930s nationalised many privileged foreign companies.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Britannica records state-controlled economic development through investment banks, state enterprises and a five-year plan, far beyond protecting people from violence.

one-party-rule.rationale: Erdogan records that the CHP was the sole governing party in 1923-1950 and that the Progressive Republican Party was closed in 1925 and the Free Party failed in 1930; in 1935 the party adopted Kemalism as its official ideology.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The 1924 constitution makes the Grand National Assembly the sole lawful representative of the nation; it makes and repeals laws, and exercises executive power through the President it elects and a Cabinet, and may withdraw power from it at any time; Clementi stresses the centrality of the Grand Assembly.

patriotic-education.rationale: Britannica records that a sense of nationalism was encouraged by changes in school curricula and the rewriting of history.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1924 constitution lists the freedom of private property among Turks' natural rights, calls property inviolable, and allows expropriation only in the public interest with prior payment, though limits may be set by law.

public-ownership.rationale: Britannica records that in the 1930s the republic moved toward state ownership or control of industry through investment banks, monopolies, state industrial enterprises and planning, with a five-year plan in 1934; private enterprise was kept, so the answer is moderate.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Britannica records the "purification" of the language by reducing the number of words of foreign origin.

reason-over-faith.rationale: In his tenth-anniversary address Atatuerk says the torch the nation holds as it marches on the road of progress is positive science; the Atatuerk centre calls Kemalist secularism rationalist.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Britannica records that clerical garb outside places of worship was forbidden in 1934; Abidor records that the fez was banned, starting with civil servants, and compares it to a headscarf ban.

religious-nation.rationale: The 1924 constitution defines "Turk" as every citizen without distinction of race or religion.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: Atatuerk's speech of 1927 says the nation would prefer to die rather than subject itself to a life of slavery.

restore-past-order.rationale: Britannica records the abolition of the caliphate, religious courts, dervish orders and the fez, as breaks with the old order.

right-to-secede.rationale: The Atatuerk centre says Kemalist nationalism holds that the Turkish state is an indivisible whole comprising its territory and people.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Erdogan records the liquidation of monarchic and theocratic institutions in 1922-1928, and Britannica records the abolition of the caliphate.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1924 constitution vests the legislature in a single Grand National Assembly.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Atatuerk centre's account of the principles says Kemalist secularism meant the separation of state and religion and also of religion from education, culture and law.

separated-powers.rationale: Under the 1924 constitution the Grand National Assembly holds legislative power and exercises executive power through the President and Cabinet it chooses and may withdraw power from, and Clementi says the constitution eroded the separation of powers.

single-official-language.rationale: The 1924 constitution declares Turkish the official language.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: The Atatuerk centre says the principle of reformism meant that Turkey replaced traditional institutions with modern institutions and eliminated traditional concepts.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The 1924 constitution places sovereignty in the nation, with the President responsible to the Assembly for high treason, and obliges all Turks to respect the law.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Britannica records state-controlled economic development achieved through investment banks, monopolies, state industrial enterprises and a five-year plan from 1934.

state-harmful.rationale: Britannica records state-controlled economic development, state enterprises and planning as a principle of the republic, which is the opposite of abolishing the state.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Atatuerk centre says Kemalist secularism was not an anti-God principle but a rationalist, anti-clerical one.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Abidor records the primacy of the state over religion, with religion no longer a visible part of Turkish life, and Britannica records the abolition of religious courts and schools in 1924.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Progressive Republican Party was closed in 1925 as a focus of counter-revolution (Erdogan), and Abidor records that Independence Tribunals went into the countryside to quell rebellion and executed the recalcitrant.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Britannica records that a purely secular system of family law was adopted for all citizens.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The 1924 constitution says the President, elected for a parliamentary term, "is eligible for re-election", with no limit stated.

women-must-cover.rationale: Abidor records the ban on the fez and the headscarf and that religion would no longer be a visible part of Turkish life.

women-suffrage.rationale: Britannica records that women were given the right to vote and to sit in parliament.

workers-own-party.rationale: The CHP programme of 1935 banned the founding of organisations based on class and class struggle (Erdogan), which shut out a separate workers' party.

missingStatements.text: The state may require citizens to change their customary dress in order to modernise society.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1925 Hat Law replaced the fez with Western hats and later laws restricted religious clothing, a defining Kemalist method of reform from above.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to the Turkish Hat Law; the dress statement covers state regulation of religious dress.

missingStatements.text: Public officials and state-school students should not wear religious dress in state institutions.
missingStatements.rationale: Laicism excluded religious symbols from the public domain, and a 1934 law restricted religious dress outside worship, though Atatürk himself did not ban the headscarf and adherents differ.

missingStatements.text: Foreign-owned concessions in key industries should be taken into national ownership.
missingStatements.rationale: The statist policies of the 1930s nationalised many privileged foreign companies and aimed at industrial self-sufficiency that would banish foreign influence.

quotes.text: industrial self-sufficiency that would banish foreign influence all stimulated a movement in the 1930s toward state ownership or control
1930’lu yıllarda devletçilik politikaları ile çok sayıda imtiyazlı yabancı şirket millileştirilmiş

notes: Brought to rules 7 in a later pass: the earlier answers rested on Wikipedia and general inference, so 208 were nulled with their old versions kept in the statements' reviewHistory, and the answers kept or changed now cite Britannica, Abidor, Erdoğan (in Turkish), the Tarsus American College pages, Atatürk's 1927 speech and tenth-anniversary address, and the 1924 constitution. Themes searched: the six principles, economy and state enterprise, class and labour, religion and secularism, dress, women and family law, the constitution and the head of state, the party system and opposition, nationalism and minorities, language and education, foreign policy and territory. The sources are silent on most questions of health, welfare, environment, technology, gender identity, animals and monetary policy, so those are null. The 1924 constitution still names Islam the state religion, so religion answers rest on later actions, not on it. Atatürk's six-day speech was read in full only for the passages quoted. Uncertainty rule likely not met.
